front: Data Center Quiz: roughly how many datacenters existed worldwide in 2011, and how much space did they occupy?
back: About 510,000 datacenters occupying about 285.5 million square feet (aggregated by datacenterknowledge.com). Current estimates are much higher, and the numbers keep changing.

front: Internet Services: what is an internet service?
back: Any type of service that is accessible via a web interface. Users communicate with it via web requests issued by their web browsers.

front: Internet Services: what are the three tiers services are most commonly divided into?
back:
• Presentation tier
  • Business logic tier
  • Database tier

front: Internet Services: what is the presentation tier responsible for?
back: Typically the static content related to the webpage layout.

front: Internet Services: what does the business logic tier do?
back: Integrates all of the business-specific processing, including all of the dynamic, user-specific content.

front: Internet Services: what does the database tier handle?
back: All of the data storage and management.

front: Internet Services: do the tiers have to run as separate processes on separate machines?
back: No. For example, the Apache HTTP web server can fulfill both the presentation tier and the business logic tier: it serves the static content, and, as part of the same process, PHP modules generate the dynamic content.

front: Internet Services: what determines whether the tiers should run as separate processes on separate machines?
back:
• The service complexity
  • The resource requirements
  • The expected loads
  • The underlying technologies

front: Internet Services: what connects and coordinates the tiers?
back: Many middleware components.

front: Internet Services: what commonly used functionality do middleware components provide?
back:
• Messaging services
  • Service configuration and management
  • Security
  • Accounting
  • Some persistence guarantees
  • Recovery management

front: Internet Services: how do multiprocess configurations communicate?
back: Via some form of IPC, such as RPC or RMI (in Java-based architectures), plus optimizations based on shared memory when different processes run on the same machine.

front: Internet Service Architectures: what does it mean to scale out a service deployment?
back: Running the service on more nodes. Multiprocess configurations are the easiest way to deal with increases in incoming request rates.

front: Internet Service Architectures: what does a front-end load-balancing component do?
back: Routes an incoming request to an appropriate or available machine that implements the internet service.

front: Internet Service Architectures: how does the load-balancer setup map onto the boss-worker pattern?
back: The front-end is the boss and the nodes are the workers, which may be general purpose or specialized.

front: Internet Service Architectures: what are the two setups possible behind a load balancer?
back:
• Homogenous: all nodes can execute any step for any request
  • Heterogenous: nodes execute some specific steps for only some request types

front: Homogenous Architectures: what can any node process?
back: Any type of request, and it can perform any of the processing actions required in the end-to-end request processing.

front: Homogenous Architectures: what is the main benefit regarding the front-end?
back: The front-end (load balancer) can be kept very simple; it does not have to track which node services which request type and can assign requests round-robin to the next available node.

front: Homogenous Architectures: how could a simple front-end still be enhanced?
back: By keeping some information about CPU loads or utilization on the other nodes and using that to direct requests.

front: Homogenous Architectures: does every node hold all of the data?
back: No. Data may be replicated or distributed across the nodes; the key point is that every node is able to get to any information necessary to execute the service.

front: Homogenous Architectures: what is a downside of this approach?
back: Little opportunity to benefit from caching; a simple front-end does not keep enough to understand the locality of each task on a node-by-node basis.

front: Homogeneous Design Quiz: in a toy shop where every worker can build any toy, how do you keep the design balanced as the order rate increases?
back: Add more of everything: more workers, work benches, and tools/parts. No decisions are needed about what the new workers do or which specific tools or parts to add, so management is fairly simple (it still takes time, but little thought goes into configuring the added resources).

front: Toy shop analogy: what do workers, work benches, and tools/parts correspond to in an internet service?
back:
• Workers: processes
  • Work benches: servers
  • Tools and parts: storage (the state needed to execute the service)

front: Heterogenous Architectures: how are nodes designated?
back: Different nodes are designated to perform certain functions or handle certain types of requests.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: give examples of how requests may be divided among servers.
back:
• By request content, e.g. the alphabetical order of the requested file name
  • eBay: servers specialized for browsing vs. bidding/buying requests

front: Heterogenous Architectures: is data required to be uniformly accessible everywhere?
back: No. Data can still live in a distributed, shared file system accessible to all nodes, but since different nodes perform different tasks, certain types of data may be much more easily accessible from the servers that manipulate those types of data.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: what is a key benefit of this approach?
back: The system can benefit from caching and locality, as each node is specialized to repeatedly perform one or a few actions.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: why does the front-end become more complex?
back: It must perform some request parsing to determine to which node it should route the request.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: why is overall management more complex?
back: When a machine fails or requests increase, you must understand which type of server needs to be scaled out; if the workload pattern changes fundamentally, the server layout must be reconfigured.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: why can't excess requests simply be redirected to idle nodes?
back: Those nodes may not be capable of processing that kind of action or serving that kind of data, even if otherwise idling. This makes it easy to end up with hotspots that have long backlogs of pending requests.

front: Heterogeneous Design Quiz: in a toy shop where each worker builds a specific toy, what must you do before adding resources as orders increase?
back: Profile what kinds of toys (requests) users are ordering and what resources each request type requires; only then can you determine exactly which workers, work benches, and parts (processes, server nodes, storage) to add. Management is much more complex than for a homogeneous design.

front: Heterogenous Architectures: which paper is a popular reference on the design space of large-scale internet services, and what tradeoffs does it describe?
back: Eric Brewer, "Lessons from Giant-Scale Services"; it describes the tradeoffs between data replication and partitioning.

front: Scale Out Limitations: using the toy shop analogy, why does adding resources stop working?
back: A single manager has limited attention and cannot control more resources, and there is a physical limit to how much staff fits in the shop. Outsourcing could help, but not if the manager only trusts their own workers.

front: Scale Out Limitations: what two limits constrain internet services from scaling out forever?
back:
• A limit on the resources that fit in a data center of a given size
  • A limit on how many things can be managed given management complexity
Running your own software stacks, OSes, and services only tightens these constraints.

front: Scale Out Limitations: what emerged to address these limits on scale?
back: Cloud computing.

front: Animoto: why was Amazon's workload in the mid 2000s imbalanced?
back: The bulk of their traffic came during the US holiday shopping season (Thanksgiving to Christmas), and much of the hardware they provisioned for that peak sat idle outside that window, or was used for other company tasks such as forecasting or other analytics.

front: Animoto: what happened in 2006 that gave birth to AWS?
back: Amazon had already built software to reprovision its machines for other services within the company; in 2006 it opened those same types of APIs to the rest of the world (web-based APIs), so third party workloads could run on Amazon resources for a fee. This was the birth of AWS and EC2.

front: Animoto: what does EC2 stand for?
back: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud.

front: Animoto: what did the company Animoto do, and why did it rent EC2?
back: It stitched together photos into a movie, a fairly resource-intensive task, so it chose to rent EC2 instances instead of building out its own datacenter.

front: Animoto: were the rented EC2 instances physical servers?
back: No, they were virtual machines; Animoto had no control over whether they ran on the same physical server or many different ones.

front: Animoto: trace the instance growth after it opened to Facebook users in 2008.
back: In April 2008 it signed up 750,000 new users in three days. Instances went from 50 (Monday) to 400 (Tuesday, an order of magnitude in a day) to 3,400 (Friday); two orders of magnitude in a week.

front: Animoto: what is the lesson of the story?
back: They could not have responded to this demand had they gone the traditional route of owning and managing their own infrastructure: they could not have brought in, installed, wired, and configured that many machines in so short a time, even with enough physical space and power.

front: Cloud Computing Requirements: how did businesses traditionally size their resources, and what was the risk?
back: They bought/configured resources based on peak expected demand. If demand exceeded expected capacity, requests had to be dropped, resulting in lost opportunity.

front: Cloud Computing Requirements: what is the ideal relationship between capacity and demand?
back: Capacity should scale elastically with demand, instantaneously, so cost is directly proportional to demand. The scaling should happen automatically, and provisioned resources should be accessible anywhere, anytime.

front: Cloud Computing Requirements: what do you give up with elastic, provider-supplied resources?
back: You do not own the resources; this may be a fair compromise.

front: Cloud Computing Requirements: list the summarized goals of cloud computing.
back:
• On-demand, elastic resources and services
  • Fine-grained pricing based on usage
  • Professionally managed and hosted
  • API-based access

front: Cloud Computing Overview: what kinds of resources does cloud computing provide?
back:
• Infrastructure resources: compute, storage, networking
  • Higher-level software resources: e.g. email, database services, or processing runtimes

front: Cloud Computing Overview: when a provider rents infrastructure resources, does it rent physical machines or disks?
back: No. It rents virtual machines, potentially interconnected into virtual clusters, along with some storage.

front: Cloud Computing Overview: why might a customer rent infrastructure together with a configured software stack instead of raw infrastructure?
back: It may be easier than renting raw infrastructure and dealing with the deployment, configuration, and management of the service yourself.

front: Cloud Computing Overview: what forms can the access/configuration APIs take?
back: Web-based, library-based, or command line-based; resources are accessed and manipulated through them over the Internet.

front: Cloud Computing Overview: name some pricing models cloud marketplaces incorporate.
back: Spot pricing, reservation pricing, or other pricing models.

front: Cloud Computing Overview: why is billing usually not done by raw usage, and what is done instead?
back: Overheads of monitoring at that fine-grained level are high, so billing uses a discrete step function; e.g. compute billed by size: tiny, medium, extra-large.

front: Cloud Computing Overview: name common software stacks for managing cloud resources.
back: The open source OpenStack and VMware's vSphere.

front: Why Cloud Computing Works: what are the two basic principles behind it?
back:
• The law of large numbers
  • Economies of scale

front: Why Cloud Computing Works: what does the law of large numbers say here?
back: Average resource needs across a large number of clients remain fairly constant, so a provider can serve many clients with variable peak loads on a fixed amount of resources, since peaks tend to be shifted in time.

front: Why Cloud Computing Works: what does economies of scale provide?
back: A provider leverages a large number of customers on a single piece of hardware, which amortizes the cost of that hardware across those customers (assuming enough customers).

front: Cloud Computing Vision: who gave the oldest description of the cloud vision, and when?
back: John McCarthy in 1961, predating the technology by almost half a century.

front: Cloud Computing Vision: what utility did McCarthy predict computing would become?
back: A public utility, like the telephone system; the computer utility could become the basis of a new and important industry.

front: Cloud Computing Vision: what does turning IT into a fungible utility mean, and what enables it?
back: Like flipping a switch for electricity without caring where it comes from, you should not need to care which hardware is used or where. Virtualization is a key enabler.

front: Cloud Computing Vision: list the limitations that keep the cloud from being a seamless utility.
back:
• Hardware dependencies that virtualization cannot fully mask
  • Different providers support different APIs (API lock-in)
  • Privacy/security concerns with external providers
  • Latency from geographic distance to resources

front: Cloud Computing Definitions Quiz: which organization published the cloud computing definition used in the lecture, and when?
back: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), October 25, 2011.

front: Cloud Computing Definitions Quiz: which phrases of the NIST definition map to elastic resources?
back: On-demand, shared pool, rapidly provisioned.

front: Cloud Computing Definitions Quiz: which NIST definition phrase maps to fine-grained pricing?
back: None (left blank): nothing in the definition talks about pricing.

text: NIST definition mapping: "{{c1::minimal management effort}}" maps to professionally managed; "{{c2::ubiquitous}}" maps to API-based access.

front: Cloud Computing Vision: is there a well-established definition of cloud computing?
back: No. There is no solid, well-established definition that the entire community subscribes to.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: who defined the different types of clouds, and what is the first dimension?
back: NIST; the first dimension is the deployment model.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: what is a public cloud?
back: The infrastructure belongs to the cloud provider, and third party customers/tenants (anyone with a credit card) rent the hardware to perform their computational tasks. Example: Amazon EC2.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: what is a private cloud?
back: The infrastructure and software are owned by the same entity; cloud technology is leveraged to keep flexibility/elasticity on in-house machines.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: give the lecture's example of a private cloud.
back: Amazon, which originally used the technology it later opened up as AWS internally, to provision its physical infrastructure elastically and dynamically across its own applications and services.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: what is a hybrid cloud?
back: A combination of public and private clouds; e.g. private clouds run the main compute, with failover/spikes handled on public cloud resources, and public clouds used for auxiliary tasks like load testing.

front: Cloud Deployment Models: what is a community cloud?
back: A public cloud that is used by certain types of users.

text: The four cloud deployment models are {{c1::public}}, {{c2::private}}, {{c3::hybrid}}, and {{c4::community}} clouds.

front: Cloud Service Models: in IaaS, which layers does the customer manage, and which does the provider?
back: Customer: applications, data, runtime, middleware, O/S. Provider: virtualization, servers, storage, networking. (PaaS: the customer manages only applications and data; SaaS: the provider manages everything; on premises: the customer manages everything.)

front: Cloud Service Models: what is Software as a Service (SaaS)?
back: The cloud provides a complete application. Example: Gmail.

front: Cloud Service Models: what is Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
back: Provides APIs and an execution environment (OS and other tools) to develop certain types of applications. Examples: Google App Engine (everything needed to develop Android applications); Windows Azure (originally, for .NET).

front: Cloud Service Models: what is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
back: The lowest level: clouds provide infrastructure instances (CPUs with memory, storage, network, possibly GPUs). Example: Amazon EC2.

text: The three cloud service models, from most to least managed by the provider, are {{c1::SaaS}} (complete application), {{c2::PaaS}} (platform/execution environment), and {{c3::IaaS}} (infrastructure instances).
extra: SaaS example: Gmail. PaaS example: Google App Engine. IaaS example: Amazon EC2.

front: Cloud Service Models: does IaaS give direct access to physical resources?
back: No, only virtualized resources, often shared with other tenants. Amazon does offer high-performance and GPU-enabled single-tenant instances where the VM runs independently on physical hardware, due to the challenge of reaching sufficient performance in a virtualized environment.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: what does it mean for cloud resources to be fungible, and why does it matter?
back: Resources can easily be repurposed to support different customers with different requirements. Without fungibility, the economic opportunity for cloud providers disappears.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: besides repurposing, what does fungibility hide from users?
back: The heterogeneity of the cloud's own resources, such as different generations or even different types of servers.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: what must resource management methods be able to do?
back: Dynamically adjust the resources allocated to cloud users depending on need, and operate at very large scale (thousands and tens of thousands of nodes).

front: Requirements for the Cloud: why is scale important for both the provider and the customer?
back:
• Provider: how many resources it must manage
  • Customer: customers often come to the cloud because they otherwise lack access to sufficiently large resource pools, so the cloud must let an individual customer allocate very large collections of resources

front: Requirements for the Cloud: why does scale make failures inevitable?
back: The probability of system failure increases with the number of components, each with an independent probability of failure. With thousands or hundreds of thousands of components, even with more reliable hardware, something somewhere will be failing.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: give the formula for the probability that at least one of n components fails if each fails with probability p.
back: 1 - (1 - p)^n

front: Requirements for the Cloud: with p = 0.03, what is the failure probability for n = 10 vs n = 100?
back: About 26% for n = 10, rising to about 95% for n = 100.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: what mechanisms deal with failures?
back:
• Timeouts for detection
  • Restart and retry for recovery
  • Backup, replication, and checkpointing

front: Requirements for the Cloud: given that failures are inevitable at scale, what attitude must cloud software take?
back: Embrace the fact that failures will happen and build robust software that can detect and recover from failures, or avoid them.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: what must multi-tenant management guarantee?
back: Performance and isolation across tenants, so a misbehaving tenant cannot wreak havoc on other tenants or the entire system.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: what must clouds guarantee about their clients' data and execution environment?
back: The privacy of the clients' data and the security of the execution environment provided to them.

front: Requirements for the Cloud: beyond tenant-to-tenant protection, which two directions do privacy and security guarantees cover?
back:
• The provider must not access or take advantage of the state managed by individual tenants
  • The platform must be protected from vulnerabilities within a single tenant, so one tenant cannot affect the entire platform

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: why is virtualization needed?
back: To provide fungible resources that can be dynamically repurposed for different customer needs.

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: which technologies address resource provisioning and scheduling?
back: mesos and yarn (Hadoop's YARN); they enable the dynamic provisioning and scheduling of the infrastructure resources.

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: which technologies handle big data processing?
back: Hadoop MapReduce and Spark, popular big data technologies that let the cloud process and store large amounts of data for customers' needs for scale.

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: what data storage technologies do cloud platforms incorporate?
back: Distributed filesystems that typically operate in append-only mode, plus NoSQL databases (a departure from traditional relational SQL databases) and storing data across distributed memories instead of repeatedly accessing disk.

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: what does it mean that cloud distributed filesystems typically operate in append-only mode?
back: Data is appended rather than arbitrarily rewritten, deleted, or modified.

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: what is needed to isolate cloud users from one another?
back: Software that can enable and configure software-defined slices of resources, so each customer thinks it owns its slice and gets its own software-defined data center (or software-defined subset of the storage or network resources).

front: Cloud Enabling Technologies: name monitoring technologies and why they are needed.
back: Flume (open source), CloudWatch (an Amazon service), Log Insight (VMware). Given the complexity of these environments, they process logs in real time and detect anomalies or failures: for the provider, to preside over the data center as a whole, and as a service to customers who want real-time, possibly interactive access to their applications' information rather than just batch access.

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: what is the key empowering benefit?
back: It empowers anyone to have potentially infinite resources: as long as you can pay, you can get the resources required to work on hard, data- and resource-intensive problems.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: how much data was created in 2011 alone?
back: 1.8 zettabytes.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: what two layers are a minimum for big-data-as-a-service?
back: A data storage layer, which stores and accesses data across many nodes, and a data processing layer, which makes it easy to describe applications in a parallel fashion so the data is processed across many nodes.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: why do these services often add a caching layer?
back: Data is brought into memory, possibly across multiple memories in the distributed system; memory access is much faster than going to disk, particularly a disk attached to another node, so repeated cache access speeds up execution.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: what else do big data stacks commonly incorporate?
back:
• A language front-end
  • Popular analytics libraries
  • Streaming support
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: why do big data stacks include a language front-end?
back: So developers can query their data in a way they are familiar with, like SQL queries or other query mechanisms.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: why do big data platforms support popular analytics libraries?
back: People want analytics and mining: searching for patterns with data mining operations that often involve common functions such as machine learning algorithms.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine: why do big data platforms need streaming support, and for what?
back: The data is often continuously generated and answers are updated continuously over time, so streaming is needed for both inputs (ingesting and staging continuously streamed data) and outputs.
source: The Cloud as a Big Data Engine

front: Example Big Data Stacks: which two open source big data stacks dominate in commercial and research settings?
back: The Hadoop stack and the Berkeley Data Analytics Stack (BDAS).

front: Example Big Data Stacks: what is HPCC, and how does it relate to Hadoop?
back: An open source big data stack by LexisNexis; it predates Hadoop but was not widely used outside of LexisNexis.

front: Example Big Data Stacks: show the Hadoop stack diagram.
Hadoop: what is the storage layer and what does it do?
back: The Hadoop file system (HDFS): it splits large amounts of data and replicates it, so data does not get lost and there are no hot spots.

front: Hadoop: what does the MapReduce processing framework do on top of HDFS?
back: Lets computation operate on the stored data and schedules data manipulation operations on specific nodes, ideally so data does not constantly have to move from one node to another.

front: Hadoop: what does HBase provide?
back: A table-like view of the stored data, similar to databases but not the same as a relational database representation.

front: Hadoop: what does the Hive language front-end do?
back: Takes an SQL query and translates it into a number of MapReduce operations on the data stored in HBase tables on top of the distributed file system.

text: Hadoop higher-level services: the {{c1::R}} environment describes how data should be processed and analyzed; {{c2::Mahout}} is a collection of machine learning algorithms.
extra: At the lowest level, all of these end up as more primitive operations executing on top of the distributed file system.

front: Hadoop: what do the supporting services provide?
back: Locking and coordination, and streaming of data into the distributed environment.

front: Example Big Data Stacks: show the Berkeley Data Analytics Stack (BDAS) diagram.
BDAS: what sits on the data storage layer, and which processing frameworks run on top?
back: An in-memory file system; on top, either the regular Hadoop MapReduce engine or Spark.

front: BDAS: which execution-model front-ends does Spark have?
back:
• SQL queries
  • Stream processing
  • Graph processing
  • Machine learning

front: BDAS: what is Mesos's role?
back: The lowest-level scheduling framework and resource manager: it partitions resources among different frameworks (e.g. a Hadoop, a Spark, and an MPI partition), which coordinate and negotiate through it, providing elasticity across very different frameworks.
